```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  echo = FALSE,

)
library(knowledge)
```

```{r load}
# data from data-raw/vignette_method.R, the methodology article's bundle
vd <- function(f) system.file("vignette-data", f, package = "knowledge", mustWork = TRUE)
x <- readRDS(vd("method.rds"))
reg <- x$settings
pk <- x$picks
sc <- as.data.frame(x$scope)
val <- function(key) gsub(";", ", ", reg$value[reg$key == key], fixed = TRUE)
n0 <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
issue <- function(n) sprintf("[#%s](https://github.com/NewGraphEnvironment/knowledge/issues/%s)", n, n)
species <- c(BT = "bull trout", CH = "chinook", CO = "coho", GR = "grayling", ST = "steelhead",
             WCT = "westslope cutthroat trout")
key_words <- function(k) {
  paste(species[[sub("_.*$", "", k)]], if (grepl("_rear$", k)) "rearing" else "spawning")
}
words_and <- function(v) if (length(v) < 2) v else paste(paste(v[-length(v)], collapse = ", "), "and", v[length(v)])
sc$share <- sc$groups_both / sc$groups
sc$margin <- sc$null_heldout_curve - sc$dev_curve
under_half <- sc$key[sc$share < 0.5]
withheld <- sc$key[sc$grade_withheld]
# a key whose curve failed has no margin, and the run withholds nothing it did not grade
curved <- sc[!is.na(sc$margin), ]
closest <- curved[which.min(abs(curved$margin)), ]
# the words: every published key drops some groups, and more than half for the keys named; the gate withholds some
# keys and publishes others, and its closest call is decided by less than one unit of deviance. A bundle without
# `scope` would make every comparison logical(0), which stopifnot() passes
stopifnot(nrow(sc) > 0, all(sc$groups_both < sc$groups), length(under_half) >= 2,
          length(withheld) >= 1, length(withheld) < nrow(sc), nrow(closest) == 1, abs(closest$margin) < 1,
          # the settings the prose quotes
          val("prior_sd") == "2.5", val("se_region") == "1", val("folds") == "5")
```

The tuning chooses the thresholds of a fish habitat definition, the few limits on a stream's size and slope that say
where a species spawns or rears, from the Province's fish sampling records, and grades each stream by how often the
species is caught on streams like it. Two textbooks set out how such a choice is made well: *Statistical Rethinking*
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking] and *Bayesian Data Analysis* [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata]. This article reads
the tuning against them: what it does as they teach, where it departs and why, and what we test next. It is a record
of where the method stands and where it is heading; the [methodology article](tuning-method.html) sets out its steps.

**The answer.** The core of the tuning is the comparison *Statistical Rethinking* teaches. Habitat definitions are
judged on watershed groups they were not fitted to, two are told apart by the uncertainty of their difference, and
the near-ties are kept together rather than reduced to one winner. It departs in three ways, each defensible for a
habitat definition whose job is to rank streams. Each left-out watershed group's own base rate is refitted before its
score is taken, so the score measures how well a habitat definition ranks streams within a group, not how many fish a
new group holds. The prior on the sampling terms is a penalty that finds one best value, not a posterior. And the
thresholds are reported as a choice and the range of close calls, not as a distribution. Three things should change:
a check meant to test the choosing does not test it, the grading curve treats an unseen sampling level unlike the
scorer, and the slopes the habitat definitions read depend on where fish were caught.

## The checks, at a glance {#glance}

Each row is one question the books raise, what the tuning does, and where that leaves it. The sections below take
them in turn.

```{r glance}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  question = c(
    "Is the score taken on data the fit did not see?",
    "Are two scores told apart by the uncertainty of their difference?",
    "Does the score predict a new watershed group?",
    "How wide is a close call, and which close call is chosen?",
    "Does the check on the choosing hold its own test data out?",
    "Is the prior a prior?",
    "Are watershed groups pooled?",
    "Which watershed group does the grade describe?",
    "Are grades withheld on a fair comparison?",
    "Is a stream's slope independent of the catch?",
    "Is a miss an absence?"),
  `what the tuning does` = c(
    "Whole watershed groups are left out of each fit and scored",
    "Yes, over watershed groups",
    "No: each left-out group's base rate is refitted first",
    "One standard error; the close call nearest link's current habitat definition",
    "No: the scores it chooses from were fitted on its test groups",
    "A normal prior on the sampling terms, fitted as a penalty",
    "Fixed in the scorer; pooled in the curve",
    "An average group",
    "A point comparison with no habitat definition",
    "No: link cuts streams at fish records",
    "A miss is read as no catch at that visit"),
  verdict = c("as the books teach", "as the books teach", "differs, defensibly", "a convention and a decision",
              "should change", "as the books teach, as a penalty", "differs", "as the books teach", "differs",
              "should change", "differs, as labelled"),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Where the tuning stands against the two books, one row per question.", row.names = FALSE)
```

## What does the tuning do? {#tuning}

For each species and life stage, the tuning builds a grid of habitat definitions around those of
[`link`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/link/) [@link], the R package that maps habitat on BC's streams: a floor on
stream size, a ceiling on slope, and for some an exception for small streams near a large river. Each habitat
definition sorts every site crews electrofished into habitat or not. A model of whether the species was caught then
asks how well that sorting predicts the catch, allowing for how much stream was fished, the data set and the period.
The **score** is how badly the model predicts the catch at sites it was not fitted to; lower is better.

The sites are grouped by **watershed group**, the Province's division of its streams into large drainages. The groups
are dealt into `r val("folds")` **folds**, and each fold in turn is left out of the fit and scored. Habitat definitions
whose scores the records cannot tell apart are **close calls**, and among them we choose the one that changes link's
current habitat definition least. A smooth **curve** of how often the species is caught, against stream size, distance
to a river and slope, then grades every stream, unless it predicts the left-out folds no better than no habitat
definition at all.

## Is the score an honest test? {#score}

A model judged on the data it was fitted to always looks better than it is: the honest test is data it has not seen.
When the data come in clusters, *Statistical Rethinking* separates two tests:

> "If we wish to validate a model against the specific clusters used to fit the model, that is one thing. But if we instead wish to compute predictions for new clusters, other than the ones observed in the sample, that is quite another." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 426]

The tuning leaves out whole watershed groups, the strict form, so no site in a scored group helped estimate how much
the habitat definition, the effort or the sampling terms matter. But before a left-out group is scored, the model refits that group's
own base rate (how often the species is caught there at all) on that group's sites. So the score asks whether the
habitat definition puts the catches on the right streams within a group, not how many catches a new group would
hold. That refit flatters every habitat definition by about the same amount, one fitted value per group, so the
comparison between habitat definitions holds while the score itself is not a prediction for a new group. It is the
right question for a habitat definition that ranks streams: how common a species is in a watershed is not the habitat
definition's to predict. The score is also taken at one best estimate, where the books average it over the posterior
[@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 210; @gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 174].

## How are two habitat definitions told apart? {#se}

Two scores are close or far by the uncertainty of their difference, not of each score alone:

> "we don’t use their standard errors but rather the standard error of their difference." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 227]

The tuning takes the standard error (SE) of each habitat definition's difference from the best over watershed groups,
the units it leaves out, as the book does over sites [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 228]. Every habitat
definition within `r val("se_region")` SE of the best is a close call, and the published table gives the range of
close calls beside the choice, closer to what the book asks than a single winner [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking,
p. 225]. The width of one SE is a convention neither book sets, and choosing the close call nearest link's current
habitat definition is a decision the scores do not make.

Choosing among thousands of habitat definitions also flatters the winner's score:

> "when these methods are used to choose a model selection, the predictive performance estimate of the selected model is biased due to the selection process." [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata, p. 182]

The book's remedy is a second level of left-out data. The tuning's check on the choosing (choosing on four folds and
scoring the choice on the fifth) was meant to be that, but the scores it chooses from came from fits that included the
fifth fold, so its test data were not fully left out. The check reports on the choosing only; it moves no choice and
no grade.

## What does the prior do? {#prior}

A prior is sceptical: it slows how fast a model learns from the sample, and keeps an estimate finite where the data
alone would let it run away. The data set and period of a record are sampling differences a habitat definition must
not be credited for, and where one data set or period caught the species every time, or never, its term ran without
bound. The tuning gives those terms a normal prior with a standard deviation of `r val("prior_sd")` on the model's
scale, the scale *Bayesian Data Analysis* uses for its default prior on such terms [@gelman_etal2013Bayesiandata,
p. 416]. It differs from that default in shape (normal rather than Cauchy, so thinner in its tails), in its link
(complementary log-log rather than logit) and in its reach (the sampling terms only, not every term).

The prior is fitted as a penalty, which finds the single most probable value and no more:

> "Ridge regression does not compute a posterior distribution." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 216]

So the tuning carries no uncertainty from the prior into its thresholds, and no simulation of what the prior implies
for the catch has been run [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 328].

## Are watershed groups pooled? {#pooling}

A model can give each watershed group its own base rate, learned from that group alone, or let the groups share what
they have in common, so a group with few sites borrows from the rest. The second, partial pooling, helps most where a
group has little data:

> "Smaller ponds produce more error, but the partial pooling estimates are better on average, especially in smaller ponds." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 413]

The scorer gives each watershed group its own base rate, which is cheap enough to score thousands of habitat
definitions and answers the within-group question above. But a group whose sites all caught the species, or none did,
has a base rate that runs to the edge and says nothing about the habitat definition, so it is dropped. For
`r words_and(vapply(under_half, key_words, ""))`, more than half the groups are dropped. The curve does pool the
groups, but it is fitted on the same groups the scorer keeps, and each left-out group is scored by its own refitted
base rate, so the pooled spread of groups never predicts one.

```{r scope}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `species and stage` = vapply(sc$key, key_words, ""),
  `watershed groups with sites` = n0(sc$groups),
  `with both catches and misses` = n0(sc$groups_both),
  `grade` = ifelse(is.na(sc$margin), "no curve", ifelse(sc$grade_withheld, "withheld", "published")),
  `curve's score less no habitat definition's` = ifelse(is.na(sc$margin), "", sprintf("%.1f", -sc$margin)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("The watershed groups each species and stage's sites fall in, the groups the scorer keeps, and",
                  "whether its grade is published: a curve whose score on the left-out folds is no lower than no",
                  "habitat definition's is withheld."),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrlr")
```

## Which watershed group does the grade describe? {#grade}

A model that pools groups can describe an average group or the spread of all of them. The grade describes an average
group, leaving each group's own base rate out [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 428], which is the right
reading for a map that compares streams across the province. Every score refits a group's base rate, so how well the
grade compares a stream in one group with a stream in another has not been tested.

## When are grades withheld? {#gate}

A curve's grades are published only when it scores lower on the left-out folds than no habitat definition at all, on
the same sites and folds. This is the comparison the books teach, and the curve's smoothness is itself penalised, so
the comparison does not count the curve's flexibility twice. But it is a point comparison with no standard error, and
the curve's variables come from the choice made on the same folds. The gate withholds
`r words_and(vapply(withheld, key_words, ""))`. Its closest call, `r key_words(closest$key)`, was
`r if (closest$grade_withheld) "withheld" else "published"` by `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(closest$margin))` in score.

## What else differs? {#else}

- **A miss is a miss at that visit.** The response is whether a crew caught the species on one visit, so a species
  present and missed reads as absent. The grade says so: it is expected use per standard electrofishing visit,
  not habitat quality. Telling the two apart needs repeat visits:

  > "In ecology, the absence of an observation of a species is a subtle kind of observation. It could mean the species isn’t there." [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 499]

- **Effort is fitted, not fixed.** The area fished enters with a fitted slope rather than as a fixed exposure, which
  lets the chance of a catch level off as more stream is fished [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 357].
- **The inputs are carried as exact.** A site's place on the stream, its slope and its modelled flow are each
  estimates. The tuning drops the worst-placed sites and reads the rest as measured, where the book carries such
  error into the model [@mcelreath2020StatisticalRethinking, p. 495].
- **A stream's slope depends on the catch.** link cuts streams at fish records, so a site that caught fish sits on a
  shorter stretch, and the slope the habitat definitions read depends on what was caught.
- **An unseen sampling level is read two ways.** At a left-out site whose data set or period the fit never saw, the
  scorer takes the reference level, the prior's centre, and the curve takes the most common one, so the gate's two
  sides treat that site differently.

## What do we test next? {#next}

- **Close the three gaps** (`r issue(203)`): the curve takes the reference level for an unseen data set or period as
  the scorer does, a run stops if the scorer ever fits a fold without its prior, and the check on the choosing is
  either nested, each fold's choice made from fits that never saw it, or described as what it is.
- **A pooled curve, scored both ways** (`r issue(186)`): a full posterior with priors on the smooths, the groups with
  only catches or only misses kept, and every left-out group scored both by its own refitted base rate and as a new
  group drawn from the spread of groups. Two cheap tests ride with it: the area fished as a fixed exposure, and a
  simulation of what the prior implies for the catch.
- **Slopes that do not depend on the catch** (`r issue(70)`): slopes over a fixed length of stream, scored against
  the field-measured slope.

## What this review did not test {#limits}

- It reads the method and fits nothing; how much each change moves a score is measured by the work that makes it.
- Occupancy models, which separate a missed species from an absent one, and the penalty scale of the smoothing
  library are named by the books but not taught there, so this review stops at what the books say.
- It describes the code and the run this article's data were written from, on `r x$meta$written` at commit
  `r x$meta$commit`.

## Software and citation {#software}

The tuning runs in the R package [`knowledge`](https://newgraphenvironment.github.io/knowledge/), on the habitat
definitions and streams of `link`. To cite this package:

```{r citation, results = "asis"}
cat(format(utils::citation("knowledge"), style = "text"), sep = "\n\n")
```
